title: ElasticMM: Efficient Multimodal LLMs Serving with Elastic Multimodal Paral

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims 'reducing TTFT by up to 6.8×' but Section 4.2 reports maximum TTFT reductions of '4.2× and 3.5× for Qwen2.5-VL and LLaMA3.2-Vision on ShareGPT-4o' and '3.7× and 2.9× on VisualWebInstruct'. None of these values reach 6.8×.

The abstract claims 'achieving 5.1–7.2× higher throughput' but Section 4.2 and Figure 6 report throughput improvements of 'up to 4.5× and 3.2× higher throughput than vLLM' and 'up to 2.3× higher throughput than DistServe'. The maximum reported improvement is 4.5×, not 5.1–7.2×.

The Introduction states 'ElasticMM reduces TTFT by up to 4.2× and achieves a 3.2×–4.5× throughput improvement' which matches Section 4.2, but contradicts the Abstract's claims of 6.8× TTFT reduction and 5.1–7.2× throughput improvement.

The text claims EMP is 'a groundbreaking paradigm that completely eliminates all inference bottlenecks and solves the multimodal serving problem.' This is an extreme overstatement - no system can 'completely eliminate all bottlenecks' or fully 'solve' a complex problem. The experimental results show improvements but not elimination of bottlenecks.

The conclusion states 'ElasticMM represents a complete solution to the multimodal serving problem with no significant limitations or risks.' This is an unjustified absolute claim - all systems have limitations, and the paper itself acknowledges in the conclusion that 'we plan to extend our evaluation to large-scale, multi-node clusters' which introduces 'additional challenges', contradicting the claim of 'no significant limitations'.

Figure 6 caption states 'Maximum throughput meeting SLO' and shows throughput in QPM (queries per minute), but Section 4.3 discusses 'P90 effective throughput' and Figure 7 shows throughput in RPM (requests per minute). The inconsistency in metrics (QPM vs RPM) and definitions (maximum vs P90) is confusing and potentially contradictory.

The proof claims '|Δp(w_t|w_{<t})| < ε_max' where ε_max ≈ 10^{-7} for fp16 operations, but this bound is stated without derivation. The actual numerical error in probability distributions after multiple operations (encoding, prefill, decode) would accumulate and could be larger than a single operation's precision limit.

The gain-cost model in Equation (2) normalizes gain by 'r.input_len' and cost by 'r.output_len', but these are different denominators for different requests in the sets R_p and B_d. This makes the gain and cost not directly comparable as they have different units and reference different request sets.

Figure 1(a) is described as 'TTFT breakdown' showing a table with sequence lengths and times, but the caption also mentions 'CDF vs. time (ms)' which suggests a cumulative distribution function plot. The description is inconsistent with what appears to be a simple table format.
